destination.title: He showed the officer the receipt and was arrested anyway

short39: He held the receipt.
Proof that the fine was already paid.
He showed it.
He was arrested anyway.
How does a man holding proof he
owed nothing end up stripped bare in a cell?
Albert Florence was driving to dinner with
his family when a trooper found an old warrant
for a fine he had paid
settled within a week.
A statewide database never cleared it.
He was arrested for a debt that
no longer existed.
At the county jail
he was strip-searched at intake.
He was moved to a second jail
and searched again
ordered to squat and cough. One stop. Two jails. Six days.
They let him go. No charges. No apology.
He sued
not for money
but on principle.
A federal court ruled for him in 2009;
an appeals court reversed it in 2010. Then in 2012
the Supreme Court disagreed
five to four:
a jail may search anyone it admits
whatever the offense.
Full story on the channel.
Follow for the cases they don't teach you.

candidate_payload_lines: "I went from having a good day with my wife standing next to me," he said, "to being scared, petrified, humiliated." He could have let it go.
On the evening of March 3rd, 2005, he wasn't driving.
Somewhere in a statewide database, no one ever pressed the key that would have erased it.
Then, in 2010, a federal appeals court reversed it.
On April 2nd, 2012, the Court gave its answer.

shorts.avoids: short39 covers the receipt, the uncleared database, the strip searches, six days, 5-4. It never mentions that he was a passenger in his own car.

lines.text: He was not driving. He was in the passenger seat, going to dinner with his family. He was arrested anyway.
source_lines: On the evening of March 3rd, 2005, he wasn't driving.

lines.text: A trooper ran the car and found a warrant for a fine. He had paid that fine. He had the paperwork with him.
source_lines: Somewhere in a statewide database, no one ever pressed the key that would have erased it.

lines.text: Somewhere in a statewide database, nobody had ever pressed the key that would have erased it.
source_lines: Somewhere in a statewide database, no one ever pressed the key that would have erased it.

lines.text: So a man riding in his own car, owing nothing, went into custody on a record that should not have existed.
source_lines: On the evening of March 3rd, 2005, he wasn't driving.

lines.text: At the county jail, booking was a procedure. It did not ask what he had done. He was ordered to remove his clothes.
source_lines: Booking is a procedure, and the procedure did not ask what he had done.
At intake he was ordered to remove his clothes.

lines.text: Days passed. He was moved to a second facility, and at the second door it happened again. One stop, two jails, six days.
source_lines: He was held. Days passed.
At the second door, it happened again.
One traffic stop. Two jails. Two searches. Six days.

lines.text: Then it ended. The payment was confirmed, and he was released. No charges. No apology. He could have let it go. He sued instead.
source_lines: No charges. No apology.
He could have let it go. Most people do.
He sued — not for the money, but on a principle: that a person arrested over a minor, unpaid fine should not be strip-searched when there is no reason at all to suspect he is hiding anything.

lines.text: The Court held, five votes to four, that a jail may strip-search anyone entering general population. Whatever they were arrested for.

lines.text: "I went from having a good day with my wife standing next to me," he said, "to being scared, petrified, humiliated."
source_lines: "I went from having a good day with my wife standing next to me," he said, "to being scared, petrified, humiliated."

lines.text: That is Albert Florence describing the evening a traffic stop turned into custody over a fine he had already paid.
source_lines: On the evening of March 3rd, 2005, he wasn't driving.

lines.text: Six days, across two facilities, on a record a database had never cleared.
source_lines: Somewhere in a statewide database, no one ever pressed the key that would have erased it.

lines.text: He could have let it go. Most people do. He took it to the Supreme Court of the United States instead.
source_lines: He could have let it go.

lines.text: By then the question was no longer only about him. It was whether a jail may search every person it admits, whatever the offense.
source_lines: The question was no longer only about him.
Not just Florence. Anyone booked.

lines.text: The majority looked at the jail door and saw danger. Correctional officers, they reasoned, cannot know who is walking in.
source_lines: The majority looked at the jail door and saw danger.
Correctional officers, they reasoned, cannot know who is walking in.

lines.text: Four dissenting justices looked at the same door and saw a person. Dignity is not nothing, they argued. The state should have some reason.
source_lines: The four dissenting justices looked at the same door and saw a person.
He argued that dignity is not nothing — that the state should have some reason before it strips a human being bare.

lines.text: Seven years later, the Court gave its answer. Five votes to four. He had won in the district court, and lost where it finally counted.
